entities.name: James of Coimbra
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jaime of Portugal, known as James of Coimbra, was a Portuguese infante (prince) of the House of Aviz, whose brief but meteoric career as a high-ranking cleric in the Roman Catholic Church spanned the mid-15th century. Born in 1433, he was the son of Infante Peter, Duke of Coimbra, a prominent regent during the minority of King Afonso V, and Isabella of Urgell. His life, though cut short by his death in 1459, exemplifies the intricate entanglement of dynastic ambition, political maneuver, and ecclesiastical power in late medieval Europe, particularly within the burgeoning Portuguese sphere of influence. He remains notable as the first cardinal from the House of Aviz, a testament to Portugal's growing international standing.

His ecclesiastical ascent began early, marked by his appointment as Administrator of the Archdiocese of Lisbon in 1453, even before his priestly ordination, a common practice for noble-born clerics of the era. This was followed by his elevation to Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata by Pope Callixtus III in 1456, at the remarkably young age of 23. This rapid promotion was largely a political maneuver, reflecting the papacy's desire to secure Portuguese loyalty and support for crusading efforts against the Ottoman Empire, as well as the House of Aviz's ambition to place its members in positions of significant European authority. James was also named Bishop of Arras in the Burgundian Netherlands, further extending his nominal influence across prominent European courts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: James of Coimbra's cardinalate marked a significant step in the House of Aviz's and Portugal's growing influence on the European stage, demonstrating the strategic use of ecclesiastical appointments for national prestige. His brief but high-profile career highlights the intricate connections between dynastic politics and the Roman Catholic Church in the 15th century.
